claim: DNS Failover consists of two components: health checks and failover.
question: What are the two components of Route 53 DNS Failover?

evidence.quote: DNS Failover consists of two components: health checks and failover.

claim: Health checks are automated requests sent over the internet to your application to verify that it is reachable, available and functional; you can make them similar to the requests your users make, such as requesting a web page from a specific URL.
question: What is a Route 53 health check?

evidence.quote: Health checks are automated requests sent over the Internet to your application to verify that your application is reachable, available, and functional.
You can configure the health checks to be similar to the typical requests made by your users, such as requesting a web page from a specific URL.

claim: With DNS failover, Amazon Route 53 returns answers only for resources that are healthy and reachable from the outside world, so end users are routed away from a failed or unhealthy part of the application.
question: Which answers does Route 53 return when DNS failover is configured?

values.display: only returns answers for resources that are healthy and reachable

evidence.quote: With DNS failover, Route 53 only returns answers for resources that are healthy and reachable from the outside world, so that your end users are routed away from a failed or unhealthy part of your application.

claim: To enable DNS failover for an ELB endpoint, create an alias record that points to the ELB and set Evaluate Target Health to true.
question: How do you enable DNS failover for an Elastic Load Balancer endpoint?

evidence.quote: To enable DNS Failover for an ELB endpoint, create an Alias record pointing to the ELB and set the “Evaluate Target Health” parameter to true.

claim: For an ELB alias with Evaluate Target Health, Amazon Route 53 creates and manages the health checks automatically, so you do not need your own health check, and the ELB health check inherits the health of the backend instances.
question: Do you need to create your own Route 53 health check for an ELB alias endpoint?

values.display: You do not need to create your own Route 53 health check of the ELB

qualifiers.scope: alias records to ELB with Evaluate Target Health

evidence.quote: Route 53 creates and manages the health checks for your ELB automatically. You do not need to create your own Route 53 health check of the ELB.
The ELB health check will also inherit the health of your backend instances behind that ELB.

claim: When failover for ELB endpoints uses alias records with Evaluate Target Health, Amazon Route 53 generates no specific CloudWatch metrics for those endpoints; use the ELB metrics, or create your own health check against the ELB name to get metrics and alarms.
question: How can you see the status of ELB endpoints when you use Evaluate Target Health?

qualifiers.scope: alias records to ELB with Evaluate Target Health

evidence.quote: Because you don't create your own health checks for ELB endpoints when using this option, there are no specific CloudWatch metrics generated by Route 53 for these endpoints.
First, Elastic Load Balancing publishes metrics that indicate the health of the load balancer and the number of healthy instances behind it.

claim: You can use DNS failover to keep a backup site, for example a static site on an Amazon S3 website bucket, and fail over to it when the primary site becomes unreachable.
question: Can a backup site be used only when a health check fails?

evidence.quote: Yes, you can use DNS Failover to maintain a backup site (for example, a static site running on an Amazon S3 website bucket) and fail over to this site in the event that your primary site becomes unreachable.

claim: The FAQ says a health check can be associated with any record type supported by Amazon Route 53 except SOA and "DNS" records, as it prints it.
question: Which record types can you associate with a Route 53 health check?

qualifiers.condition: FAQ wording; the second excluded type is printed as DNS records

evidence.quote: You can associate any record type supported by Route 53 except SOA and DNS records.

note: The FAQ prints DNS records, probably a typo for NS records. Compare with the developer guide before the writer states the second type.

claim: For ELB and S3 website endpoints, Amazon Route 53 creates and manages the health checks automatically when you create an alias record with Evaluate Target Health enabled; for all other endpoints you give the DNS name or the IP address in the health check.
question: Can you health check an endpoint if you do not know its IP address?

values.display: either the DNS name (e.g. www.example.com) or the IP address

evidence.quote: For these endpoint types, Route 53 automatically creates and manages health checks on your behalf which are used when you create an Alias record pointing to the ELB or S3 website bucket and enable the "Evaluate Target Health" parameter on the Alias record.
For all other endpoints, you can specify either the DNS name (e.g. www.example.com) or the IP address of the endpoint when you create a health check for that endpoint.

claim: You can set up health checks for parts of an application running outside AWS and fail over to any endpoint you choose, regardless of location, for example from an on-premises legacy application to a backup instance in AWS.
question: Can DNS failover be set up for an endpoint that is outside AWS?

evidence.quote: Just like you can create a Route 53 resource record that points to an address outside AWS, you can set up health checks for parts of your application running outside AWS, and you can fail over to any endpoint that you choose, regardless of location.

claim: Amazon Route 53 does not make routing decisions based on the load or available capacity of your endpoints, so you must make sure the other endpoints have capacity or can scale to take the traffic of a failed endpoint.
question: After a failover, does Route 53 consider the load on the remaining healthy endpoints?

values.display: does not make routing decisions based on the load

evidence.quote: No, Route 53 does not make routing decisions based on the load or available traffic capacity of your endpoints.

You will need to ensure that you have available capacity at your other endpoints, or the ability to scale at those endpoints, in order to handle the traffic that had been flowing to your failed endpoint.

claim: By default an endpoint is considered failed after three consecutive failed health check observations, and Route 53 resumes sending traffic after it passes three consecutive observations.
question: How many consecutive failed observations make a Route 53 health check endpoint count as failed by default?

values.display: threshold of three health check observations

evidence.quote: The default is a threshold of three health check observations: when an endpoint has failed three consecutive observations, Route 53 will consider it failed.
However, Route 53 will continue to perform health check observations on the endpoint and will resume sending traffic to it once it passes three consecutive observations.

claim: You can change the health check failure threshold to any value between 1 and 10 observations.
question: What range can the health check failure threshold have?

evidence.quote: You can change this threshold to any value between 1 and 10 observations.

claim: When a failed endpoint passes the configured number of consecutive observations (default three), Route 53 restores its DNS records automatically and traffic resumes with no action required.
question: How is DNS failover reversed when a failed endpoint becomes healthy again?

values.display: no action required on your part

evidence.quote: After a failed endpoint passes the number of consecutive health check observations that you specify when creating the health check (the default threshold is three observations), Route 53 will restore its DNS records automatically, and traffic to that endpoint will resume with no action required on your part.

claim: By default, health check observations are conducted at an interval of 30 seconds.
question: What is the default interval between Route 53 health check observations?

qualifiers.condition: a fast interval can be selected

evidence.quote: By default, health check observations are conducted at an interval of 30 seconds.

claim: You can optionally select a fast interval of 10 seconds between health check observations, which means three times more checks and three times the requests to your endpoint.
question: What is the fast health check interval, and what does it cost the endpoint?

evidence.quote: You can optionally select a fast interval of 10 seconds between observations.
Fast interval health checks also generate three times the number of requests to your endpoint, which may be a consideration if your endpoint has a limited capacity to serve web traffic.

claim: Each health check runs from multiple locations around the world, and an endpoint should expect about one request every 2-3 seconds for standard interval checks and one or more per second for fast-interval checks.
question: How much load does a Route 53 health check put on an endpoint?

qualifiers.condition: based on the current default number of health checking locations

evidence.quote: Each health check is conducted from multiple locations around the world.

Based on the current default number of health checking locations, you should expect your endpoint to receive one request every 2-3 seconds on average for standard interval health checks and one or more requests per second for fast-interval health checks.

claim: Health checks do not follow HTTP redirects: they treat an HTTP 3xx code as a successful response.
question: Do Route 53 health checks follow HTTP redirects?

values.display: HTTP 3xx code to be a successful response

evidence.quote: Route 53 health checks consider an HTTP 3xx code to be a successful response, so they don’t follow the redirect.

claim: For string matching health checks, avoid pointing the health check at a location that returns an HTTP redirect, because the check searches for the string in the body of the redirect and never reaches the target.
question: Why can a redirect cause unexpected results in a string matching health check?

values.display: avoid pointing the health check at a location that returns an HTTP redirect

evidence.quote: The health check searches for the specified string in the body of the redirect.
For string matching health checks, we recommend that you avoid pointing the health check at a location that returns an HTTP redirect.

claim: When a health check fails and failover occurs, Amazon Route 53 disables the resource records for the failed endpoint and stops serving them, so traffic goes to the healthy endpoints.
question: What happens in the failover step when a health check fails?

values.display: disables the resource records for the failed endpoint

qualifiers.condition: after three consecutive failed checks by default

evidence.quote: Route 53 disables the resource records for the failed endpoint and no longer serves these records.

claim: The FAQ recommends a TTL of 60 seconds or less when using DNS failover, to shorten the time before traffic stops going to a failed endpoint.
question: What TTL does the FAQ recommend for records used with DNS failover?

evidence.quote: We recommend a TTL of 60 seconds or less when using DNS Failover, to minimize the amount of time it takes for traffic to stop being routed to your failed endpoint.
